bp: Many text classifiers now use a large language model by putting a few labeled examples and an instruction into the prompt, then asking the model to label a new message. This is attractive because a team can build sentiment, toxicity, or illicit-promotion classifiers without training a separate model from scratch. The paper asks whether that convenience creates a security hole. In a real deployment, the person submitting text may not be cooperative. A spammer, toxic user, or illicit promoter wants the classifier to read a dangerous message as harmless. ICL-Evader studies that setting under a strict condition: the attacker does not inspect the model's weights, see its internal calculations, or test many guesses against the live system. The central object is therefore not just a text label. It is the whole prompt-processing situation: examples, instruction, candidate text, and the model's tendency to treat some prompt evidence as more important than other evidence.
wh: The hard part is that in-context learning depends on reading a bundle of words as a temporary rulebook. The model must infer from the examples what counts as positive sentiment, toxicity, or illicit promotion, then apply that inferred rule to the new text. A defender may assume this is safer than a brittle keyword list because the model can understand paraphrase. But the same flexibility means the model can be steered by text that looks like ordinary context. An attacker who cannot query the model cannot tune a custom attack from feedback, so the attack has to exploit more general weaknesses in how these models handle prompts. The abstract names three such routes: fake claims, templates, and needle-in-a-haystack placement. Each targets a different confusion: believing misleading stated context, following a surface pattern, or losing the important evidence inside a long surrounding prompt. Defending is hard because fixing one confusion may leave the others open.
naive: A smart beginner would first write a clear prompt with good examples and trust the model's general language skill to apply the labels. If attacks appear, the beginner might add stronger wording such as do not be fooled, or might test older text attacks that swap words while preserving meaning. That fails for two reasons in this paper's setting. First, the attacker needs no model feedback, so defenses that rely on catching repeated probing do not help. Second, ordinary word-level attacks are not aimed at the special weakness of in-context prompts: the model is judging both the submitted text and the surrounding prompt cues. The attack can therefore change the decision by changing what the prompt seems to imply, not merely by hiding a bad word.
ap: The core idea is to treat in-context classification as an exposed reading procedure rather than as a sealed classifier. ICL-Evader builds attacks that do not need to learn the victim model's private details. Instead, they use general prompt tricks that are likely to disturb many large language models because those models must compress a long context into a decision. Fake Claim appears to add misleading claims that compete with the real task evidence. Template appears to exploit repeated prompt forms that the model may follow too mechanically. Needle-in-a-Haystack appears to bury decisive material among distracting context so the classifier gives the wrong part too much or too little weight. After showing that these attacks harm sentiment, toxicity, and illicit-promotion classification, the paper turns the same diagnosis into defense. It studies multiple protections and combines them into a joint recipe, then packages the recipe as an automated tool for strengthening standard in-context prompts.
mech: The mechanism starts with a normal in-context classification prompt: task instructions, a small set of labeled examples, and one new text to classify. The attacker receives no model weights, no internal score, and no trial-and-error response from the target while constructing the attack. Instead of searching through feedback, the attacker rewrites or wraps the input using one of three designs. In the Fake Claim route, the submitted text is made to carry a misleading assertion that pressures the model toward an attacker-preferred label. In the Template route, the text is shaped so it fits a form the model may imitate or over-trust, pulling the decision away from the intended label rule. In the Needle-in-a-Haystack route, the important malicious or label-changing material is placed where long-context reading is likely to dilute it among irrelevant material. The attacked prompt is then passed to the classifier, and success is measured by whether the label changes in the attacker's favor on tasks such as sentiment analysis, toxicity detection, and illicit-promotion detection. The defense side reverses the process. It tests candidate protective strategies against all three attack families, looks for a combination that blocks the shared weaknesses, and turns that combination into a tool that rewrites or fortifies ordinary in-context prompts before deployment.
math: The main mathematical idea is adversarial evaluation: instead of asking only how often the classifier is right on clean examples, define a contest in which one side changes the input to increase mistakes and the other side changes the prompt to reduce them. In plain terms, this is a search over ways to make a reading task fail. The unusual feature is the zero-query black-box condition. Black-box means the attacker treats the model as hidden; zero-query means the attacker cannot keep trying candidate prompts and learning from returned labels during construction. That changes the math from feedback-guided tuning to transfer by structural weakness: attacks are designed around prompt-processing patterns expected to hold across models. Classification itself is a scoring problem, even when the abstract does not expose the exact score: the model compares possible labels and emits one. The attacks try to alter which evidence in the prompt receives practical weight. The defenses are another constrained search. They must reduce attack success while keeping ordinary classification accuracy nearly intact, so the tradeoff is security versus utility. The reported less-than-five-percent accuracy loss matters because a perfect shield that ruins normal labels would not be useful.
dots: This paper belongs to the repo's LLM adversarial robustness thread, but it also connects to several broader conference ideas. It is a security paper because an opposing user is actively choosing inputs that make a system misclassify. It is a language-model paper because the vulnerable object is not a trained classifier alone but the model's temporary rule-following from prompt examples. It connects to optimization because both attacker and defender are choosing prompt changes under constraints: the attacker has no queries, and the defender must preserve normal accuracy. It also neighbors misinformation, toxicity, and illicit-content work because those are settings where small wording changes can change platform decisions. Compared with graph or retrieval poisoning papers in the local data, the surface object is text rather than links or documents, but the deeper shape is shared: useful context can be turned into an attack surface when the system cannot reliably decide which context deserves trust.
ww: The attack works when the model's strength, flexible reading of context, becomes a liability. A fixed keyword filter can be crude, but it has fewer ways to be persuaded by surrounding language. An in-context classifier is more capable because it infers the task from examples and instructions each time. That means extra claims, familiar templates, and buried evidence can compete with the intended decision rule. The zero-query setting is plausible because these weaknesses are not tiny model-specific cracks found by repeated probing; they are broad habits of prompt processing. The defense works only if it addresses the different habits together. A rule that removes irrelevant noise may help against buried distractions but may not stop a fake claim. A stronger instruction may help against misleading context but may not fix template following. The joint defense recipe is therefore sensible: it reduces several routes by which attacker text can be treated as decision evidence, while trying not to damage the useful evidence that clean in-context learning needs.
po: The payoff is a practical security assessment of prompt-based text classifiers. The paper shows that under a strict no-query attack model, ICL-Evader can sharply degrade classification, with the abstract reporting attack success as high as 95.3 percent and traditional NLP attacks doing poorly under the same constraints. It also gives defenders something operational rather than only a warning: a studied combination of defenses that mitigates all three attack families with less than five percent accuracy degradation, plus an automated tool for fortifying standard in-context prompts before they are exposed to adversarial users.
limits: Several assumptions must hold. The attacks rely on general prompt-processing weaknesses being present in the target large language model and task prompts; a model or prompt design that handles long context and conflicting claims differently may be less affected. The defense claims are grounded in sentiment, toxicity, and illicit-promotion tasks, so the abstract does not prove the same protection for every classification domain. It also does not show complete immunity, only mitigation with small utility loss. Because the input abstract is truncated at the end, details about datasets, models, exact prompt rewrites, and deployment conditions cannot be verified from this file alone.
